summary: Describes how to carry redundant copies of audio data in RTP packets, so that if a packet is lost the sound can be rebuilt from a later one. A packet holds the current audio plus a lower-quality copy of earlier audio. This helps voice calls survive packet loss on the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: When you talk over the internet, some words can get lost. This trick tucks a quiet copy of the last words into the next message so gaps can be filled in.

subtitle: How to pack lower-quality copies of earlier audio into each RTP packet so lost packets can be patched up.

tldr.problem: Packet loss badly hurts the intelligibility of speech in Internet audio conferences, even at low loss rates.
tldr.mechanism: One RTP payload type acts as a container. Each packet carries the current (primary) audio plus one or more redundant copies of earlier audio, each preceded by a small header giving its encoding, age and length.
tldr.outcome: If a packet is lost, the receiver can rebuild the missing audio from the redundant data in a following packet. The format is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6354.

facts.label: Redundant block header
facts.value: 32 bits: F 1, block PT 7, timestamp offset 14, block length 10

today: RFC 2198 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 6354. Read the two together.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2198 defines an RTP payload format for redundant audio data, for use with version 2 of the real-time transport protocol (RTP). The authors were building audio conferencing tools for lossy packet networks such as the Internet Mbone, although the scheme is not limited to that.

The most significant quality problem they identified was packet loss, which disrupts speech intelligibility even at low loss rates. Their answer is to add redundancy to the data stream. If a packet is lost, the missing information can be rebuilt from redundant data that arrives in the following packet or packets, provided the average number of consecutively lost packets is small.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone calls over the internet drop bits of sound. To fix that, each message also carries a small backup copy of the sound before it.

sections.title: Why a Container Payload Type
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC lists the requirements and explains the choice. A packet has to carry a primary encoding and one or more redundant encodings. Each block needs an encoding type identifier and a length indicator, because variable-size encodings are desirable. Redundant blocks cover different time intervals, so each needs its own timestamp, which can be sent compactly as a difference from the primary timestamp.

The RFC weighs the options. An RTP header extension would let applications that ignore redundancy skip it, but it costs 4 bytes of extension header plus up to 3 bytes of padding, and it limits a packet to a single redundant encoding unless more structure is added. Defining a dynamic payload type for every primary/redundant combination does not scale once multiple blocks of redundancy are needed, and agreeing on a fixed working set of 32 combinations out of band is complicated.

The preferred solution is a single payload type that marks a packet with redundancy. That packet is a container for several payloads, each preceded by a header saying what it holds. It is flexible, extensible and has relatively low overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing a new kind of envelope for every mix of backups, there is one big envelope with labelled pockets inside.

sections.title: The Redundancy Block Header
sections.content:
A redundant packet has a standard RTP header whose payload type indicates redundancy. The other RTP header fields relate to the primary block. After the RTP header come the additional headers, one per block, then the data blocks themselves.

Each header for a redundant block is 32 bits with four fields: F (1 bit, 1 if another header follows and 0 if this is the last), block PT (7 bits, the RTP payload type of the block), timestamp offset (14 bits) and block length (10 bits, in bytes, excluding the header).

The timestamp offset is unsigned and is subtracted from the RTP header timestamp to get the time of the data the block protects. So redundancy must be sent after the primary data, never before. The offset is measured in the same units as the primary timestamp, so the redundant encoding MUST be sampled at the same rate as the primary.

The odd 14 and 10 bit split is deliberate. An 8 bit length is not enough for some encodings, for example 80ms PCM and DVI audio packets of more than 256 bytes. Adding a sign bit to the offset would shrink its range unacceptably.
sections.plainLanguage: Each backup copy gets a little label that says what kind of sound it is, how long ago it happened and how big it is.

sections.title: Primary Block and Packing Rules
sections.content:
The primary encoding block header is placed last. Its timestamp and length can be worked out from the RTP header and the overall packet length, so it is only 8 bits: a zero F bit and the 7 bit block payload type.

The data blocks follow the last header immediately, in the same order as the headers, with no padding or delimiter. The headers are 32 bit aligned but the data typically is not. This saves bandwidth at the cost of some extra decoding time.

If a packet carries several redundant encodings, they should cover different time intervals. The redundant encoding is expected to use significantly less bandwidth than the primary, and it MUST NOT be higher bandwidth than the primary. The exception is a very low-bandwidth primary with high processing cost, where a copy of the primary MAY be used as the redundancy. Multiple levels of redundancy are rarely needed, and each level should need significantly less bandwidth than the previous one.
sections.plainLanguage: The main sound goes last with a tiny label. The backups go first, and each one should be smaller than the main sound.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content:
The RTP marker bit is not preserved for redundant blocks. If the primary packet carrying the marker is lost, the marker is lost. The authors argue this is acceptable because even a marker sent with the redundant data could be lost, so applications must cope with that anyway.

CSRC information is not preserved either. The CSRC data in the RTP header relates only to the primary. Because CSRC data in an audio stream is expected to change relatively infrequently, applications that need it are advised to assume the header's CSRC data also applies to the reconstructed redundant data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some small details, like a flag on the main message, are not copied into the backups. The receiver just has to live with that.

sections.title: Describing Redundancy in SDP
sections.content:
The RFC leaves payload type assignment out of scope: an RTP profile may assign one, otherwise a dynamic payload type is chosen. A common way to bind a dynamic type is the Session Description Protocol (SDP) rtpmap attribute. For redundancy the codec name is red.

The m= line lists the payload types a receiver must be ready to use. When redundancy is used, those formats are also taken to be the only codecs allowed in the redundant encodings. To receive a redundant stream, that is all that is needed.

To send one, the sender needs to know which codecs to use for the primary, secondary and further encodings. This is carried in an fmtp attribute whose parameters are a slash-separated list of RTP payload types. Encodings cannot be named in fmtp unless they are also valid on the m= line. In the RFC's example, 0/5 means PCM as primary and DVI as secondary.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a call starts, both sides agree in writing which sound types are allowed and which one is the main one and which is the backup.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Redundant packets are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification and the relevant RTP profile, so confidentiality comes from encrypting the media stream. Encryption can be applied to the whole stream in the usual way, or a portion of the stream can use a different key. In the second case a redundant copy of the last packet of that portion cannot be sent, because no following packet uses the right key to carry it. Similar limits can appear when encryption is turned on or off. The choice is up to the encoder, and decoders need no change.

The RFC also warns that adding large amounts of redundancy increases congestion and therefore packet loss, which worsens the problem it was meant to solve. At worst this can cause excessive congestion and may constitute a denial of service attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Backups only help if you do not overdo them. Too many copies clog the road and make even more messages get lost.

sections.title: Example Packet
sections.content:
The RFC's worked example is an RTP packet with a DVI4 (8KHz) primary and a single block of redundancy encoded with 8KHz LPC, both covering 20ms packets. After the RTP header come two headers: the first has F=1, block PT 7 (LPC), plus a timestamp offset and block length for the redundant block; the second has F=0 and block PT 5 (DVI4) for the primary.

The data follows in the same order: 14 bytes of LPC redundant data, then 84 bytes of DVI4 primary data.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, a small 14-byte backup rides along in front of an 84-byte main sound.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: 1 if another header block follows, 0 if this is the last.

fields.name: block PT
fields.desc: RTP payload type of this block.

fields.name: timestamp offset
fields.desc: Unsigned offset subtracted from the RTP timestamp.

fields.name: block length
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the data block, excluding the header.
